sentences: It is midday in spring, and a quiet farmhouse yard has suddenly erupted.
The title means "breaking the stillness," and that is exactly what happens here.
This one small sheet of paper holds shrieks, flapping wings and shouting, all at the same moment.
The painter is Kim Deuk-sin, a court painter of the late Joseon period.
He came from a whole family of court artists, including his uncle, his brothers and his sons.
He carried on Kim Hong-do's style of genre painting, full of wit about ordinary lives.
Start with the wild cat.
It dashes off with a chick in its mouth, yet even mid-escape it turns its head to glance back at the chaos it has caused, completely unbothered.
The strong contrast of black and white draws your eye there first.
Right behind comes the mother hen, wings spread wide, in pursuit.
Robbed of her chick, she launches herself off the ground and charges desperately at the thief.
You can almost hear the frantic beating of her wings.
The other chicks scatter in every direction.
Each tiny body runs a different way, and together they spread the commotion across the whole yard.
Even the smallest creatures here are full of movement.
The man of the house lunges off the wooden veranda, swinging his long tobacco pipe.
In his hurry to stop the cat he has thrown himself forward with no thought for his footing.
Imagining the next second, we cannot help laughing.
Behind him, his wife rushes out barefoot.
There was clearly no time even to put on her shoes.
We can almost hear her startled cry, as if sound and motion had been caught right there on the paper.
The picture is painted on paper only about 27 centimeters wide.
Quick ink lines set down each shape, and light washes of color are laid over them, so the whole scene feels airy, fresh and alive.
It belongs to an album of Kim's genre scenes in the Kansong Art Museum.
The album gathers eight humorous pictures of ordinary people's lives, and in 2018 it was designated a national Treasure of Korea.
Some read the cat as a stand-in for the petty officials who preyed on ordinary people.
Above all, though, the picture shows the joy of genre painting, freezing one ridiculous second of village life so well that you can almost hear it.
Step back and take it all in again.
Whose side are you on: the cool cat, the frantic master, or the furious hen?
Try imagining the noise that filled this yard for that one second.
